I seem to be rather unique among my group of friends/acquaintances, because I have never felt the need to have the question of the existence of God answered. As a child, my parents were neither religious or atheists- they just didn't discuss religious things at all. Our lives went by with no real need for it. For any 'where does-the-world-come from' type questions growing up, my father encouraged me to discover scientific explanations for such questions. My grandmother tried to convert me to the LDS faith when I was 7-10, but I quickly found the whole thing ridiculous, largely because I have never really needed to know about whether there is a God or not. I have met many people who are devout Christians, and many who are die-heard atheists, and some agnostics, but I have never found another person in real life who simply didn't find the question important.

Don't get me wrong, I have deeply pondered questions about the origins, meaning, and possible future of the universe-- I just never really felt the need to determine whether there was a God. I am in constant wonder at the things I have come to know about the world, and I revel in the joy of existence. I am awed by the infinite play of form, energy, and matter that makes up everything-- from a tear on dying child's cheek, to the toothless smile of an old woman, to the brightness of a sun rise over the ocean, to the mechanics of blackholes and exploding supernovas. I remember learning about thinkers of the Enlightenment, and especially striking to me was the idea of God as a 'watchmaker' -- on who creates 'the machine' and just then lets it run without directly interfering. For me, the important part of this idea is the machine, not the watchmaker.

When I read Kant's ideas about "the unknowability of the thing in itself", this idea came back to me-- that the 'watchmaker', if it exists, is so remote and different from our own existence as to be unfathomable to us. Any of the things commonly attributed to God, such as omnipotence and omnipresence, are things that by the very fact of our existence as the creatures we are, are not comprehensible to us. If God exists, any attempts to understand or relate to it in any way would be as futile as asking one of the cells in our body to 'understand' our raison d'etre or life goals, or asking the cell to believe in our consciousness. And asking this God-being to care about any human suffering would be as useless asking a person to be aware of and care about the individual sufferings or death of a single one of their cells. Sure, if enough cells die, we will feel the distress, but not because we care that those cells died-- except insofar as it could endanger our continued existence.

I have never really cared whether God exits or not. Most people I know cannot abide this-- they need for there to be a god, or else ultimately their will to live is threatened, or they need to affirm that there is no God, as though ultimately their will to live is threatened if the God-delusion is allowed to stand. But I have never met anyone for whom it simply was not a relevant question to ask at all.
